data.name: CreateSubtitle
data.value: Encrypt your files into a chunk-based backup. Only you, with your password, can read them.

data.name: UpdateSubtitle
data.value: Refresh an existing backup with the latest changes. Only modified chunks are re-encrypted.

data.name: RestoreSubtitle
data.value: Decrypt a backup and restore the original files to any folder.

data.name: SettingsSubtitle
data.value: Defaults for new backups and application language.

data.name: AboutSubtitle
data.value: Quick guide to using BackupZCrypt and a reference for the available algorithms.

data.name: HelpCreateText
data.value: Pick the source folder and an empty destination folder (or one holding a previous backup, which is replaced only once the new one is complete). Type a strong password —or press Generate— and confirm it. Then press “Start backup”.

data.name: HelpUpdateText
data.value: Select the current source folder and the existing backup. Files whose size and date have not changed are kept without being read again, and only changed chunks are re-encrypted, so it is much faster than rebuilding the backup. Files deleted from the source are also removed from the backup; you are told which ones before anything changes.

data.name: HelpRestoreText
data.value: Pick the backup folder (the one containing manifest.bzc) and the folder where you want the files restored. You will be asked for the backup password.

data.name: HelpVerifyText
data.value: Pick the backup folder (the one containing manifest.bzc) and enter its password. BackupZCrypt checks every chunk and tells you whether the backup is intact — without restoring anything. Damaged chunks are set aside so that Update can rebuild them from the source.

data.name: HelpPasswordText
data.value: The password is the only way to decrypt a backup: if you lose it, the data cannot be recovered. Keep it in a password manager. The strength meter helps you choose a robust one.

data.name: HelpSettingsText
data.value: Open “Settings” in the sidebar to choose the encryption, key derivation, and compression for new backups, as well as the language. If in doubt, keep the defaults. The benchmark estimates how long a backup would take on your computer with the options you choose. Existing backups always keep their own algorithms.

data.name: DefaultsNote
data.value: They apply to new backups. Each existing backup keeps the algorithms it was created with, and BackupZCrypt detects them automatically when you update, restore, or verify it.

data.name: DestinationHint
data.value: Empty folder where the backup will be written…

data.name: RestoreDestinationHint
data.value: Folder where files will be restored…

data.name: EncryptionIntro
data.value: Protects the contents of your files. All five options use 256-bit keys and authenticated encryption, which also detects any tampering, and none has a known practical attack. The choice mainly affects speed.

data.name: KeyDerivationIntro
data.value: Turns your password into the encryption key. It is slow on purpose, so that every guess is costly for an attacker, but it runs only once per operation and adds a few seconds at most. Even so, what protects you most is a long, unique password.

data.name: CompressionIntro
data.value: Shrinks your data before it is encrypted. It saves a lot of space with text, code, databases, and programs, but photos, videos, music, ZIP files, and Office documents are already compressed and barely shrink.

data.name: NoneCompressionSummary
data.value: Default. The fastest; ideal for photos, video, and music.

data.name: NoneCompressionDescription
data.value: Data is encrypted as is. It is the fastest option and the right one when most of your files are already compressed (photos, videos, music, ZIP files, or Office documents), because compressing them again would hardly save any space.

data.name: DetectMissing
data.value: No backup was found in this folder.

data.name: DetectFound
data.value: Encrypted backup found. Enter its password to continue.

data.name: LanguageRestartNote
data.value: Language changes apply after restarting the application.

data.name: AesDescription
data.value: The worldwide encryption standard and the most thoroughly studied cipher. Almost every current processor has dedicated AES instructions, which make it the fastest option. Choose it unless you have a specific reason to use another.

data.name: AesSummary
data.value: Recommended (default). The fastest on almost any computer.

data.name: SerpentDescription
data.value: Runner-up in the competition that produced AES, designed with a deliberately generous security margin: it applies 32 rounds of encryption where AES applies 14. In exchange, it is the slowest option. Choose it if maximum caution matters more to you than speed.

data.name: SerpentSummary
data.value: Very conservative design. The slowest option.

data.name: CamelliaDescription
data.value: Developed in Japan by Mitsubishi Electric and NTT, with security comparable to AES. It is approved by ISO/IEC and was selected by the EU's NESSIE project and Japan's CRYPTREC. Choose it if you want a recognized standard that does not come from the United States. It runs purely in software here, which makes it much slower than AES.

data.name: ChaCha20Description
data.value: A modern cipher designed to be fast without help from the hardware, used in TLS 1.3 and WireGuard. It is the fastest alternative to AES on this list and the best choice on older or low-power processors that lack AES instructions. On other computers, AES is usually somewhat faster.

data.name: ChaCha20Summary
data.value: Modern and fast, even without AES acceleration.

data.name: TwofishDescription
data.value: One of the five finalists of the competition that produced AES. Its internal design is very different from AES's, so it is a sensible choice if you prefer not to depend on AES. It runs purely in software here, which makes it much slower than AES or ChaCha20.

data.name: TwofishSummary
data.value: AES finalist with an independent design. Slower.

data.name: Pbkdf2Description
data.value: A veteran standard (NIST SP 800-132) that repeats HMAC-SHA256 800,000 times. It needs almost no memory, so an attacker with graphics cards can try many more passwords per second than with Argon2id or Scrypt. Its main advantage is being on NIST's list of approved algorithms: if you do not need that, choose Argon2id, and if you do choose it, use a long password.

data.name: Pbkdf2Summary
data.value: NIST-approved, but the least resistant to GPU attacks.

data.name: Argon2idDescription
data.value: The recommended variant of Argon2, winner of the Password Hashing Competition, and the method that OWASP and RFC 9106 advise today. Each password attempt needs 256 MB of memory, which makes large-scale attacks with graphics cards or specialized hardware very expensive. It is the right choice for almost everyone.

data.name: Argon2idSummary
data.value: Recommended (default). The best protection against attacks.

data.name: ScryptDescription
data.value: The first key-derivation function designed to demand a lot of memory (2009), and still a solid choice: here it also uses 256 MB per attempt. Argon2id, which is newer, better withstands some advanced attacks. Choose it if you prefer an algorithm with a longer track record.

data.name: ZstdFastDescription
data.value: Zstandard at level 1. It saves almost as much space as Normal and compresses somewhat faster. Useful for large amounts of data when backup time matters more than space.

data.name: ZstdFastSummary
data.value: Compresses faster than Normal, but saves a little less.

data.name: ZstdDescription
data.value: Zstandard at level 3, its standard setting. It compresses well while staying fast, so it is the best choice when your data includes a good amount of text, code, databases, or programs.

data.name: ZstdSummary
data.value: Good balance of savings and speed. Recommended for text, code, and databases.

data.name: ZstdBestDescription
data.value: Zstandard at level 19. It produces the smallest backups, but compressing takes tens of times longer than with Normal, even for files that will not shrink. It is only worth it if storage space is very tight and your data compresses well. Restoring stays fast, because decompression speed barely depends on the level.

data.name: ZstdBestSummary
data.value: The smallest backups, but much slower compression.
